nameStory: The 'marsh' in marsh-bedstraw refers to this plant's love of wet, soggy places where many other plants can't survive. The 'bedstraw' name comes from medieval times when people would stuff mattresses with dried plants from this family - the stems and leaves created a springy, somewhat comfortable sleeping surface.
description: Common marsh-bedstraw is a delicate, low-growing annual plant that spreads across wet ground like a green carpet. It has tiny white flowers and narrow leaves arranged in neat whorls around square stems. The whole plant rarely grows taller than 8-12 inches, but it can spread widely through marshes and wet meadows, creating dense mats.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in whorls of 4-6 around the stem, like spokes on a wheel. Run your finger along a leaf - they're smooth with slightly rough edges and feel thin and delicate.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers, barely 1/8 inch across, with 4 petals that form a perfect cross shape. They appear in small clusters at leaf joints and have a faint, sweet fragrance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms sprawling mats that hug the ground or lean on nearby plants for support. The stems are weak and often tangled together, creating a loose, messy appearance.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that feel smooth when you roll them between your fingers. They're often reddish at the joints where the leaf whorls attach.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces tiny, smooth, round fruits that turn from green to brown. They're so small they look like pinhead-sized beads attached to the stem.

habitat: Look for marsh-bedstraw in wet meadows, marshy areas, pond edges, and boggy spots throughout New England. It thrives in consistently moist to wet soils and is often found growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other moisture-loving plants. You'll rarely find it in dry upland areas.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small green shoots in wet areas. The characteristic whorled leaves become visible as the plant begins to spread.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time with tiny white cross-shaped flowers appearing from June through August. This is the best time for identification when flowers and full leaf whorls are present.
seasonality.fall: Plants begin to turn yellow and brown as seeds mature. The delicate stems become more brittle and tangled.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving no above-ground traces. Only seeds remain to sprout the following spring.

funFact: Despite being classified as a noxious weed in six New England states, marsh-bedstraw is actually native to the region and has been here longer than European settlement - it's one of the few plants that's both native and legally considered a pest!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small bedstraws, especially three-petal bedstraw which grows in similar wet areas. The key difference is the flower petals - marsh-bedstraw always has 4 petals in a cross shape, while three-petal bedstraw (despite its name) usually has 3 tiny petals.
contextualKnowledge: Though called a 'noxious weed' in New England, this classification seems to be based on its aggressive spreading habit in wetlands rather than it being a harmful introduced species. The legal designation can be confusing since the plant is actually part of the region's natural heritage.
compareHints: Marsh-bedstraw is distinguished from other bedstraws by its preference for consistently wet habitats and its delicate, mat-forming growth pattern. Unlike the climbing catchweed bedstraw with its scratchy stems, or the upright lady's bedstraw with yellow flowers, marsh-bedstraw stays low and spreads horizontally across wet ground. Its 4-petaled white flowers also help separate it from the 3-petaled species in the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bedstraws, catchweed is unique for its extremely clingy nature and annual growth habit.

Hedge bedstraw differs from other common bedstraws by its smooth stems and purely white flowers - catchweed bedstraw has sticky stems, lady's bedstraw has yellow flowers, and fragrant bedstraw has a sweet vanilla scent when crushed.
Unlike its weedy cousin catchweed bedstraw which grabs onto your clothes with hooked bristles, sweet woodruff stays put and feels soft to touch.
Among New England's bedstraws, fragrant bedstraw is unique for its sweet vanilla scent when crushed – most other bedstraws are odorless or have different scents.
Among New England's 15+ bedstraw species, licorice bedstraw stands out with its consistently four broad, oval leaves per whorl - most others have 6-8 narrow, linear leaves arranged in circles.
Lady's bedstraw stands out among New England's bedstraws because of its bright yellow flowers - most other bedstraw species have white or greenish blooms.
Among New England's bedstraws, rough bedstraw is distinguished by its prominent stem hooks and preference for wet areas.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw with its velcro-like sticky stems or sweet woodruff's hay-like fragrance, Torrey's wild licorice has smooth stems and that distinctive taste.
Unlike catchweed bedstraw which has sticky, grabby stems and four-petaled flowers, three-petal bedstraw feels smoother and has its distinctive three-petaled blooms.
Among the 15+ bedstraw species in New England, stiff marsh bedstraw is one of only two with 3-petaled flowers (the other being three-petal bedstraw).
Among New England's bedstraws, hairy bedstraw is unique for its consistently soft, fuzzy texture throughout the plant.

White bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and smooth stems - catchweed bedstraw has hooked bristles that grab onto clothing, while lady's bedstraw has bright yellow flowers instead of white.
Unlike the common catchweed bedstraw with its grabby, rough stems, boreal bedstraw is soft and non-sticky.
Northern bedstraw differs from other New England bedstraws by its upright growth habit and narrow leaves with three parallel veins.
Among New England's bedstraws, bluntleaf bedstraw stands out for its preference for wet habitats and those distinctive rounded leaf tips.
